thread.title: GameStop's Failure To Transform - GameStop Corp. (NYSE:GME)

author: Strubel Investment Management
title: GameStop's Failure To Transform - GameStop Corp. (NYSE:GME)
text:
Over the last six years, GameStop (NYSE: GME ) stock has lost about half its value. We were bullish on the company many years ago, but its rudderless strategy for a digital world caused us to sell our final holdings (we had aggressively trimmed the position prior to that) in 2016.
GameStop has wasted tremendous amounts of money on stock buybacks, acquisitions, and dividends over the past years. The company had significant opportunities to make transformative acquisitions but missed out or passed on them. While things are bad for the company now, it’s still not too late to pursue a different strategy.
A (Almost) Decade Wasted The chart below shows GameStop’s share price over the past six years. We’ve highlighted in red just how high the shares rose during a time when the company was continually buying back stock.
From FY2012 to FY2017 the company repurchased over $1.2B in stock. The company also raised its dividend and made over $800M in acquisitions. Despite all this, the company still receives 71% of its gross profit from traditional physical game and hardware sales and the stock price has been cut in half. Even worse, the company sacrificed their balance sheet to achieve this. In FY2012 they had $636M in cash and no long term debt. Today their net cash position is almost entirely eliminated by long term debt ($864M in cash less $818M in long term debt).
As we mentioned earlier, the company repurchased a total of $1,278M in stock over the past six years. The company also raised its dividend. It now spends about $150M per year paying dividends compared to $102M six years ago. The dividend cost the company a total of $846M. It also spent $886M on acquisitions.
Not all of the acquisitions worked out or seemed logical. For example, the company bought gaming platform Kongregate for a rumored $12M to $40M only to turn around several years later and sell it for $55M. While it made money on the sale, which is nice, it didn’t do anything to bring GameStop into the new digital era. Other acquisitions like Spawn Labs weren’t as successful and were closed down completely.
They also bought over 500 AT&T Mobility stores and bought several Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) product retailers. Seemingly following the dying retailer playbook of attempting to use other company’s success to jumpstart their own. They spent $140M buying ThinkGeek. A nice business, perhaps, but nothing gamechanging or truly transformative.
GameStop could have been in a much better position if it had made wise investments. The video game world is thriving. People are spending more time playing games, e-sports is rising in popularity, and the stocks of video game publishers has soared (partially due to distributing direct to consumers and cutting out physical retailers like GameStop). GameStop could have been an integral part of all of this.
What Could Have Been Imagine what GameStop could have been if it took all of the cash it spent on buybacks, all of the cash it spent on an increased dividend, and all of the cash it spent on acquisitions and branched out wisely. Subtract out the extra debt it took on and the company would have about $1,580M ($1278M from no buybacks, $234M from not raising the dividend, $886M from acquisitions, less $818M in debt) it could have spent.
They could have bought Twitch back in August of 2014 for $970M (when Amazon bought it) or if they had bought it in 2013, it was only valued at $100M . Although that was the series C valuation so a buyout after that likely would have to have been at a premium. They could have made investments in game studios. Respawn Entertainment was acquired for $455M , Riot Games cost $400M in 2011, a 40% stake in Epic Games cost $330M in 2013. Polish studio CD Projekt SA traded at about $500M in 2013. If GameStop wanted to take on that $800M or so of debt, Take-Two Interactive (NASDAQ: TTWO ) would have even been a possibility as it traded at only $10 a share several times in 2010 and 2012 (a 100% premium would put the price at $2.3B).
The company could have even made a run at a stake in Valve or tried to by the Steam portion of the company. Given Valve’s founder owns about 50%, an outright sale of Valve would be unlikely, but there were rumors of a $1B price tag being associated with Steam back in 2011.
Imagine a GameStop today that owned Steam plus has a stake in Valve or a GameStop that owns Twitch plus has a decent sized game publishing division. Or simply a GameStop that realized it was being dis-intermediated and now has moved up the value chain to the publishing position.
It’s Not Too Late The ship has obviously sailed on some of these opportunities. Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN ) owns Twitch now. It’s doubtful GameStop could afford to buy Steam today and Take-Two’s market cap dwarfs anything GameStop could afford. But, it’s not too late to just move up the value chain and build a publishing business. GameStop generates about $250M per year in free cash flow after all. That’s a decent chunk of change the company has every year to start doing something to prepare for the next era of gaming. Slashing the dividend, which at this point may be a good idea, would give the company another $150M a year or so.
With company currently searching for a new CEO, GameStop has a chance to bring in someone with a coherent vision for the future that isn’t based on selling physical games and gaming related tchotchkes . Until then we think GameStop stock remains uninvestable.
Disclosure: I am/we are long TTWO, EA, ATVI, AMZN.
